newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa's de Klerk denies running criminal regime.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa's de Klerk denies running criminal regime.

text.p: Former South African president F.W. de Klerk denied on Wednesday that he had run a criminal regime during the apartheid era and denounced police hit-squads as cold-blooded murderers.
De Klerk, under cross-examination by the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, renewed his apology for apartheid but said he had committed no crime for which he required amnesty.
He said he had been as shocked as anyone by disclosures in recent weeks of murders, kidnappings and torture sessions by senior police officers in applications for amnesty.

But in one heated exchange with commission lawyer Glen Goosen, de Klerk refused to answer questions on a defence force document apparently condoning assassinations of black activists. He said he needed time to study it and would reply later.
Asked by Goosen if his National Party presided over a period of "state-sanctioned criminal activity", de Klerk said: "I reject that formulation with every fibre of energy."
He said his government had operated within an ethos that the law had to be upheld. "Inasmuch as that philosophy was violated, it is a dark blotch on our history."
De Klerk said a document produced by Goosen detailing a discussion by cabinet ministers on whether "terrorists" should be wiped out by their own methods did not represent government thinking.
"During my presidency I went out of my way to get to the bottom of the truth and to find and prosecute the perpetrators of dastardly deeds," de Klerk said.
"I have never condoned gross violations of human rights and reject any insinuation that it was ever the policy of my party or my government."
De Klerk said maverick policemen who objected to his steps to dismantle apartheid since 1990 were responsible for some of the atrocities that had been committed.
His bodyguards feared such police officers might try to kill him. "They were as much against the reforms as they were against the African National Congress (ANC)," de Klerk said.

Goosen asked him to comment on a series of notorious security force actions over the last three decades, including the activities of the "Vlakplaas" police hit squad and the recently discovered bodies of 12 assassinated ANC activists.
De Klerk said such actions were "absolutely unacceptable" and fell outside what a policeman or soldier could have interpreted government policy to have been.
Goosen said a police general and three colonels had applied for amnesty after confessing to having killed the 12.

"I was not in favour of changing the law to allow cold-blooded murderers to go free," de Klerk replied, referring to negotiations with the ANC that led up to South Africa's first all-race elections in 1994 and also provided for the kind of amnesties now being offered.
He said he had agreed to the amnesty provisions at the urging of the ANC, who he said had wanted to protect its own guerrillas.
Commission head Archbishop Desmond Tutu interjected that the list of actions presented by Goosen extended over a long period and involved people of senior rank.
"It becomes difficult to see how one can sustain a position that it was just a few bad eggs," Tutu said.
Goosen said the commission had heard evidence of 1,200 separate acts of torture by apartheid security forces and the practice appeared to have been systematic and routine.
De Klerk repeated an earlier acknowledgment by the National Party that it accepted responsibility for having created "an atmosphere conducive to human rights violations" by police.
"(The police) had to fight a revolutionary onslaught which had as its...goal to make South Africa look like Zaire is looking today...It was underground, it used terrorist methods.
"The result was more authority to security forces to fight the war, a very specific type of war," de Klerk said.

The truth commission was set up in 1995 to uncover as much as possible of the human rights abuses and crimes committed by all sides during apartheid. Earlier this week it questioned the ANC about its activities.
